key_terms.meaning: q = τ t, shear force per unit length of wall, in N/mm.
The point a transverse load must pass through for the beam to bend without twisting.
e = 3b²/(h + 6b) outside the web, on the side away from the flanges (uniform t).
q<sub>s</sub> = −[(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D]∫t x ds − [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D]∫t y ds, from q = 0 at a free edge.
q₂ − q₁ = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>) B<sub>r</sub> y<sub>r</sub> across boom r (symmetric section).
q<sub>s</sub> = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>s,0</sub>; for zero twist q<sub>s,0</sub> = −∮(q<sub>b</sub>/t)ds/∮ds/t.
q = T/2A; τ = q/t; dθ/dz = (T/4A²G)∮ds/t; J = 4A²/∮ds/t.
T = Σ2A<sub>R</sub> q<sub>R</sub>; equal dθ/dz in every cell; shared wall carries q₁ − q₂.
B = stringer area + Σ(t b/6)(2 + σ₂/σ₁) over the panels it touches.
S<sub>y,w</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> − ΣP<sub>z,r</sub> δy<sub>r</sub>/δz; two-boom spar: q = (S − M h′/h)/h.
q<sub>b</sub> from free edges and one cut per cell; a constant only in closed cells.
σ<sub>t</sub> = 2W/(t d sin 2α); flanges lose W/(2 tan α) each; stiffener load W b tan α/d.
J = Σbt³/3; τ<sub>max</sub> = T t/J; dθ/dz = T/GJ.

takeaways: Shear flow q = τ t is set by the shear force, through the change of bending stress along the beam; it is zero at free edges and continuous round corners.
The shear centre is a property of the section; a load anywhere else adds a torque equal to the load times its offset.
A closed section is cut, solved as open, and given a constant q<sub>s,0</sub> fixed by moments or by zero twist.
Under pure torque one closed cell carries q = T/2A in every wall; several cells share the torque and twist at one rate.
Booms carry direct stress and panels carry shear; a good idealisation reproduces the exact I<sub>xx</sub>.
In a tapered beam the inclined booms carry part of the shear, so the web carries S − M h′/h, not S.
A buckled web carries shear as diagonal tension, which compresses the flanges, loads the stiffeners and bends the flanges between them.
Open sections are a hundred or more times weaker in torsion than a closed section of the same material.
bank_note: Long questions usually ask for the shear flow distribution and shear centre of a channel or box, Bredt–Batho torsion of a single or two-cell section, the shear flow in an idealised or tapered wing box, or Wagner's tension field. Draw the section with the cut and the direction of s, state the sign convention, and check that the flows add up to the applied shear.

glossary.def: q<sub>b</sub>, the flow in a closed section after it has been cut, found as for an open section.
A concentrated area that carries all the direct stress of a stringer or spar cap and its share of skin.
The theory of torsion of thin-walled closed sections: q = T/2A, constant round the cell.
One closed loop of walls in a section; a wing box with a middle spar has two.
The point about which a section rotates under pure torque; it coincides with the shear centre.
Wagner's idealisation of a buckled web that carries all its shear as diagonal tension.
Tension along the wrinkles of a buckled shear web, at angle α to the flanges.
Said of a wall whose skin is counted in the booms or carries direct stress; one that is not is ineffective in bending.
An unconnected edge of an open wall, where the shear flow is zero.
Replacing a stiffened section by booms carrying direct stress and panels carrying shear.
A length of skin or web between booms, carrying a constant shear flow in the idealised section.
dθ/dz, the twist angle per unit length, in rad/mm or rad/m.
The point through which a transverse load produces bending without twist; also called the flexural centre.
Shear force per unit length of wall, q = τ t, in N/mm.
A web that carries its shear without buckling.
τ<sub>cr</sub>, the shear stress at which a flat web panel wrinkles.
Torsion of a member whose cross-section warps freely; for open thin walls J = Σbt³/3.
A vertical member on a web that holds the flanges apart and anchors the tension field.
The change of depth or width of a beam along its span; it inclines the booms.
J in dθ/dz = T/GJ; 4A²/∮ds/t for a closed cell, Σbt³/3 for an open section.
Axial displacement of points of a cross-section under torque, so that it does not stay plane.

bank.q: Define shear flow and shear centre. Explain why a load through the shear centre bends a beam without twisting it, and derive the shear-centre position of a channel of uniform thickness.
outline: q = τ t and its origin in dM/dz
answer: Shear flow. In a thin wall the shear stress τ is taken as uniform through the thickness t, so the wall transmits a force per unit length q = τ t, in N/mm. It is set by the shear force: the bending stress changes along the beam at a rate set by dM/dz = S, and q balances that change on any piece of wall cut off from a free edge.

answer.text: For a section symmetric about x, measuring s from a free edge, with y the signed coordinate:
answer.pre:
q(s) = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>) ∫₀ˢ t y ds
q = 0 at a free edge; linear along a flange; parabolic along a web

answer: Shear centre. The flows q ds add up to a single force equal to the applied shear. Its line of action depends only on the section shape. The point through which the lines for every shear direction pass is the shear centre. A load through it produces bending only; a load elsewhere is equivalent to the same load at the shear centre plus a torque equal to the load times its offset, and the beam twists.

Sketch: a channel with the web vertical and the flanges pointing right; the shear centre is drawn a distance e to the left of the web, on the horizontal axis of symmetry; flows run along the top flange towards the web, down the web and out along the bottom flange.

answer.text: Derivation of e for a channel with web h, flanges b and uniform t. With the flange second moment about its own axis neglected:
answer.pre:
I<sub>xx</sub> = t h³/12 + 2 (b t)(h/2)² = t h²(h + 6b)/12
flange flow at the corner:  q<sub>j</sub> = (S/I<sub>xx</sub>) t b (h/2)
flange force:  F = q<sub>j</sub> b/2 = S t b² h/(4 I<sub>xx</sub>)

answer.text: The two flange forces are equal and opposite, a couple F h. Moments about the web mid-line:
answer.pre: S e = F h   →   e = t h² b²/(4 I<sub>xx</sub>) = 3b²/(h + 6b)

answer: Numbers: for h = 120 mm, b = 60 mm, t = 3 mm and S = 5 kN, I<sub>xx</sub> = 1,728,000 mm⁴, q<sub>j</sub> = 31.25 N/mm, F = 937.5 N and e = 22.5 mm.

Centroid against shear centre. The centroid of the same channel is x̄ = 15.0 mm from the web on the flange side. A load through the centroid is 37.5 mm from the shear centre and twists the channel with T = 5000 × 37.5 = 187,500 N·mm.
Special cases: doubly symmetric sections have the shear centre at the centroid; singly symmetric ones on the axis of symmetry; sections whose walls meet at one point (angle, tee) at that point.
Use in design: ribs, hinge brackets and control surfaces are arranged so that loads pass close to the shear centre, or the section is closed into a box, which can carry the resulting torque.

bank.q: Derive the expression for the shear flow in a thin-walled open section under shear forces S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub>, and explain how the shear centre is found. Include sections with stiffening booms.
answer: Set-up: a thin open wall of thickness t, mid-line coordinate s from a free edge, centroidal axes x and y, bending moments M<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>y</sub>, shear forces S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub> with dM<sub>x</sub>/dz = S<sub>y</sub> and dM<sub>y</sub>/dz = S<sub>x</sub>. There is no axial load.

answer.text: Equilibrium of a wall element ds × dz along the beam: the direct stress σ on the two faces differs by (∂σ/∂z) dz and the shear flow on the two edges by (∂q/∂s) ds. With no axial load:
The unsymmetrical bending stress gives ∂σ/∂z in terms of the shear forces:
answer.pre:
σ = [(M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] x + [(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] y,   D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>²
∂σ/∂z = [(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] x + [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] y

answer.text: Integrating from the free edge, where q = 0:
answer.pre: q<sub>s</sub> = −[(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫₀ˢ t x ds − [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫₀ˢ t y ds

answer: Special case: a section symmetric about x under S<sub>y</sub> alone gives q<sub>s</sub> = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫t y ds.
Assumption: the shear acts through the shear centre, so the section does not twist; a load elsewhere adds a torsion flow.

Procedure: (1) centroid and the three second moments; (2) pick a free edge and the direction of s; (3) write x(s) and y(s) for each wall; (4) integrate wall by wall, carrying the end value of one wall into the next; (5) check zero at the other free edge and that the walls sum to S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub>.

answer.text: Worked check, the Z-section of the open-section chapter (web 80 mm, flanges 40 mm, t = 2 mm, S<sub>y</sub> = 3 kN): I<sub>xx</sub> = 341,333, I<sub>yy</sub> = 85,333, I<sub>xy</sub> = 128,000 mm⁴. The flow runs:
answer.pre:
top flange tip → corner:  0, 5.02, 4.02, −3.01, −16.07 N/mm
web peak at the neutral axis:  −48.21 N/mm
bottom flange back to 0 at its tip

answer: The sign changes inside each flange show the effect of I<sub>xy</sub>; the web carries 3000 N and each flange zero net force.

answer.text: Stiffening elements: if booms carry the direct stress and the walls carry only shear, the integral is replaced by jumps:
answer.pre: q₂ − q₁ = −[(S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] B<sub>r</sub> x<sub>r</sub> − [(S<sub>y</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] B<sub>r</sub> y<sub>r</sub>

answer: Shear centre: take moments of all the q ds about a convenient point (a corner where several walls meet removes them from the sum) and equate them to the moment of the shear force placed at the unknown shear centre, once for S<sub>y</sub> (giving its x coordinate) and once for S<sub>x</sub> (giving its y coordinate). For the stiffened channel of the chapter this gives 26.67 mm outside the web.

bank.q: State and derive the Bredt–Batho theory for torsion of a thin-walled closed tube: shear flow, shear stress, rate of twist and torsion constant. Apply it to a rectangular wing box.
answer: Assumptions: thin closed wall, pure torque T, no axial stress, the cross-section keeps its shape and warps freely.

Constant q. Cut a rectangular wall element with edges along the beam and round the section. With no direct stress, equilibrium along the beam requires the shear flows on its two longitudinal edges to be equal. So q is constant round the cell, even where t changes.

answer.text: Torque. A length ds at perpendicular distance p from any point O carries a force q ds with moment q p ds. Since p ds is twice the area of the thin triangle from O:
answer.pre:
T = ∮ q p ds = q ∮ p ds = 2 A q   →   q = T/(2A)
τ = q/t = T/(2 A t)

answer: A is the area enclosed by the mid-line; τ is largest where t is smallest.

answer.text: Rate of twist. The complementary energy of the wall per unit length is ∮q²/(2Gt) ds; equating its rate of change with the work of T per unit length, (1/2)T dθ/dz, or summing the displacements round the loop, gives:
answer.pre:
dθ/dz = (1/2A) ∮ q/(G t) ds = (T/4A²G) ∮ ds/t
J = 4A²/∮ds/t,   dθ/dz = T/(G J),   θ = T L/(G J)

answer: Check for a thin circular tube: A = πR², ∮ds/t = 2πR/t, J = 2πR³t, the polar second moment of a thin ring; τ = T/(2πR²t) agrees with T r/J at r = R.
Numbers, the single-cell box of the Bredt–Batho chapter: mid-line 600 × 200 mm, skins 1.5 mm, spar webs 3 mm, T = 30 kN·m, G = 27 GPa. A = 120,000 mm², q = 30 × 10⁶/(2 × 120,000) = 125 N/mm.
τ = 83.3 N/mm² in the skins and 41.7 N/mm² in the webs; ∮ds/t = 800 + 133.33 = 933.33; J = 6.171 × 10⁷ mm⁴.
dθ/dz = 1.800 × 10⁻⁵ rad/mm = 1.03° per metre; over 4 m, 4.13°.

Why the thin walls carry the stress: q is the same in every wall, so τ = q/t is largest where t is smallest; the designer therefore sizes the thinnest skin for strength and uses ∮ds/t, dominated by the thin walls, for stiffness.
Check of the box numbers by the integral form: (1/2AG)∮q ds/t = 125 × 933.33/(2 × 120,000 × 27,000) = 1.800 × 10⁻⁵ rad/mm, the same rate as T/GJ.
Limits: the theory loses accuracy as the wall thickens; warping restraint at a root rib stiffens the box; a buckled skin carries shear as a tension field; several cells need the multi-cell equations.

bank.q: Explain the structural idealisation of a stiffened wing section into booms and panels. Derive the effective boom area and show that the idealised section reproduces the bending stiffness.
outline: Walls effective and ineffective in bending
answer: Why idealise: a stiffened skin has direct stress varying continuously round the section, and integrating the shear flow round dozens of stringers by hand is long. Most of the direct stress is in the stringers, spar caps and the skin next to them; the thin skin between them is good in shear.
The idealised section: booms of area B at the stringer and spar-cap positions carry all the direct stress; panels of the real thickness t between booms carry only shear, constant along each panel.

answer.text: Derivation of the boom area. A skin panel of width b and thickness t has a linear direct stress from σ₁ at edge 1 to σ₂ at edge 2. Replace it by areas B₁ and B₂ at the edges that give the same moment about edge 2:
answer.pre:
σ₁ B₁ b = σ₂ t b (b/2) + (1/2)(σ₁ − σ₂) t b (2b/3)
B₁ = (t b/6)(2 + σ₂/σ₁)

answer: Each boom collects this term from every panel it touches plus its own stringer area.

Ratios: a skin panel between two booms at the same height under bending has σ₂/σ₁ = 1 and gives t b/2 to each boom; a spar web from the top to the bottom boom has σ₂/σ₁ = −1 and gives t b/6; for pure axial load every ratio is 1.
Example: a box 400 × 200 mm, spar caps 300 mm², mid-width stringers 150 mm², skins and webs 2 mm. Corner: 300 + (2 × 200/6) × 3 + (2 × 200/6) × 1 = 566.7 mm². Mid stringer: 150 + 2 × 200 = 550 mm².

Check: Σ B y² = (4 × 566.7 + 2 × 550) × 100² = 3.3667 × 10⁷ mm⁴, exactly the I<sub>xx</sub> of the real section (skins 1.6 × 10⁷, webs 2.667 × 10⁶, caps and stringers 1.5 × 10⁷). That is why the idealised section gives nearly the same stresses as the real one: it has the same bending stiffness by construction.

Using it: boom stresses σ = M y/I<sub>xx</sub>; panel flows from the jumps q₂ − q₁ = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)B y at each boom, with q<sub>s,0</sub> added in closed cells. For 15 kN in the example, each top and bottom skin panel carries 12.25 N/mm and each web 37.5 N/mm.

Limits: the stress ratio depends on the load case (bending, axial, combined), so the booms change with it; the skin between stringers in compression may buckle and carry less than assumed; shear lag in wide skins puts more stress near the webs than the linear stress assumption.

Walls effective and ineffective in bending: a wall whose skin is included in the booms carries shear only in the idealised model but is effective in bending through the booms; a wall left out of the booms is ineffective in bending. Both appear in ∮ds/t.

bank.q: A channel has a web 150 mm deep and flanges 75 mm wide, all 2 mm thick (mid-line dimensions). It carries a vertical shear of 6 kN. Find and sketch the shear flow distribution, locate the shear centre, and find the torque if the load acts through the centroid.
answer: Data: channel with web h = 150 mm, flanges b = 75 mm, t = 2 mm throughout (mid-line), S<sub>y</sub> = 6 kN vertical; flange second moment about its own axis neglected.

answer.text: Second moment:

answer: Top flange, s from the free tip (y = +75): q = (S/I<sub>xx</sub>) t y s in magnitude = (6000/2,250,000) × 2 × 75 × s = 0.40s. Linear, from 0 at the tip to q<sub>j</sub> = 30.00 N/mm at the corner (s = 75).

Web, s₂ down from the corner (y = 75 − s₂): q = 30.00 + (S/I<sub>xx</sub>) × 2 × (75s₂ − s₂²/2). Parabolic, peak at the neutral axis: q = 30.00 + (6000/2,250,000) × 2 × 75²/2 = 45.00 N/mm; back to 30.00 N/mm at the bottom corner.
Bottom flange: linear from 30.00 N/mm at the corner to 0 at the free tip.

Checks: the web carries 2 × (30.00 × 75 + (2/3)(15.00) × 75) = 6,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>; each flange carries a horizontal force F = q<sub>j</sub> b/2 = 30.00 × 75/2 = 1125.0 N, the two in opposite directions.

Sketch: triangles on the two flanges (zero at the tips), a parabola on the web with its peak at mid-depth; arrows along the top flange towards the web, down the web, out along the bottom flange for a downward shear.

answer.text: Shear centre, moments about the web mid-line (the web passes through it):

answer: The shear centre lies 28.12 mm from the web mid-line on the side away from the flanges, on the horizontal axis of symmetry.
Centroid: x̄ = (2 × 150 × 37.5)/(2 × 150 + 300) = 18.75 mm from the web, on the flange side.

A load through the centroid is therefore 46.88 mm from the shear centre and adds T = 6000 × 46.88 = 281,250 N·mm = 281.25 N·m, which the open channel carries poorly (its J is only Σbt³/3 = 300 × 8/3 = 800 mm⁴).

bank.q: A rectangular box has a mid-line 300 mm wide and 150 mm deep, a 3 mm front wall, a 2 mm rear wall and 1.25 mm skins. Using the cut-and-add method under a vertical shear of 20 kN, find the shear flow distribution and the position of the shear centre.
answer: Data: rectangular box, mid-line 300 mm wide and 150 mm deep; front wall 3 mm, rear wall 2 mm, top and bottom skins 1.25 mm. S<sub>y</sub> = 20 kN. Find the shear centre. The section is symmetric about x, so the shear centre lies on the x axis and one load case is enough.

answer.text: Second moment:

answer: Cut the front wall at mid-height; s runs up the front wall, along the top, down the rear wall, back along the bottom. q<sub>b</sub> = −k∫t y ds.

answer.text: Corner values of q<sub>b</sub>:
answer.pre:
top-front:  −k × 3 × 75²/2 = −30.00 N/mm
top-rear:   −k × (8,437.5 + 1.25 × 75 × 300) = −130.00 N/mm
bottom-rear: −130.00 N/mm (the rear wall adds +, then −)
bottom-front: −30.00 N/mm, and 0 again at the cut

answer.text: Twist integrals ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds/t, wall by wall:

answer: Wall forces ∫(q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>s,0</sub>) ds: front wall 10,810 N upwards, rear wall 9,190 N upwards, top and bottom skins 619.8 N each along s. Vertical check: 10,810 + 9,190 = 20,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>.

answer.text: Moments about the mid-point O of the front wall (anticlockwise positive):

answer: Shear centre: x<sub>S</sub> = M<sub>O</sub>/S<sub>y</sub> = 133.2 mm behind the front wall, 16.8 mm forward of mid-width. The thick front wall takes 54.0 per cent of the shear and pulls the shear centre towards itself.
Comparison: the centroid is at x̄ = 135.0 mm, so here the shear centre and centroid are 1.8 mm apart; they must be found separately.
A lift of 20 kN acting at mid-width would add a torque 20,000 × 16.8 = 335,950 N·mm, carried as an extra constant flow T/2A = 3.73 N/mm round the box.

bank.q: A wing D-nose cell is a semicircle of 150 mm mid-line radius (skin 1.2 mm) closed by a 300 mm spar web (2.5 mm). It carries 6 kN·m. With G = 27 GPa find the shear flow, the shear stresses, J, the rate of twist and the twist over 3 m.
answer: Data: wing leading-edge D-cell, a semicircular nose of mid-line radius 150 mm (skin 1.2 mm) closed by a spar web 300 mm deep (2.5 mm). Torque 6 kN·m, G = 27 GPa, length 3 m.

answer.text: Enclosed area and ∮ds/t:
Shear flow and stresses:

answer: The thinner nose skin carries the larger stress although the flow is the same in both walls.

answer.text: Torsion constant and twist:

answer: Check by the first form of the twist formula: (1/2AG)∮q ds/t = 84.88 × 512.7/(2 × 35,342.9 × 27,000) = 2.280 × 10⁻⁵ rad/mm, the same.

Sensitivity: the nose skin contributes about three-quarters of ∮ds/t, so thickening it is the efficient way to stiffen the cell; doubling the web thickness alone would cut ∮ds/t only from 512.7 to 452.7, about 12 per cent.
If the allowable shear stress of the skin is 100 N/mm², the torque capacity is limited by the nose: T<sub>allow</sub> = 2A t τ = 2 × 35,343 × 1.2 × 100 = 8.48 kN·m.

Comparison with a rectangle: a 300 × 300 mm square cell of the same 300 mm depth would enclose 90,000 mm², about 2.5 times as much, and carry the same torque with q = 33.3 N/mm. The D-nose is chosen for the aerofoil shape, not for torsional efficiency, and is usually combined with the box behind it, as in the next question.

Order of work in an exam: draw the cell with its mid-line, mark the thickness of each wall, compute A, then ∮ds/t wall by wall, then q, τ in each wall, J and the twist. State G and the units of each line (N, mm, rad).
Shear modulus check: G = E/2(1 + ν) = 70,000/(2 × 1.33) = 26,300 N/mm² for ν = 0.33, so the 27,000 N/mm² used here is typical of aluminium alloys; with 26,300 the twist would be 0.0702 rad.
Assumptions: thin walls, free warping, no buckling of the nose skin, shape held by ribs.

bank.q: The D-nose cell of the previous question is joined at its spar to a rectangular cell 500 mm × 300 mm with 1.5 mm skins and a 2.0 mm rear spar. The section carries 40 kN·m. Find the shear flows in all walls and the rate of twist (G = 27 GPa).
answer: Data: a two-cell wing section. Cell 1 is the D-nose of question 7 (A₁ = 35,343 mm², nose skin 1.2 mm). Cell 2 is a rectangle 500 mm × 300 mm behind it (A₂ = 150,000 mm²) with 1.5 mm skins and a 2.0 mm rear spar. The front spar, 300 mm deep and 2.5 mm thick, is shared. T = 40 kN·m, G = 27 GPa.

answer.text: Wall integrals:
Rates of twist, cell flows anticlockwise, the shared wall carrying q₁ − q₂:
answer.pre:
dθ/dz (cell 1) = (δ₁ q₁ − δ₁₂ q₂)/(2 A₁ G)
dθ/dz (cell 2) = (δ₂ q₂ − δ₁₂ q₁)/(2 A₂ G)

answer.text: Equal twist and the torque equation:

answer: The first gives q₁ × (0.015306) = q₂ × (0.009640), so q₁ = 0.6298 q₂.
Shared spar: q₁ − q₂ = −42.98 N/mm, that is 42.98 N/mm in the sense of cell 2; τ = 17.2 N/mm².
Outer walls: nose τ = 60.9 N/mm², cell 2 skins 77.4 N/mm², rear spar 58.1 N/mm².
Torque shares: cell 1 carries 2A₁q₁ = 5.17 kN·m, cell 2 carries 34.83 kN·m.
Check against one cell: had the rear cell alone carried the torque, q = 40 × 10⁶/300,000 = 133.3 N/mm. The nose cell takes a share, and the shared spar carries only the small difference.

Physical check of the shared spar: it carries the difference of two nearly equal circulations, so it is lightly loaded in torsion; its stress of 17.2 N/mm² is far below the nose skin stress of 60.9 N/mm². In shear, by contrast, the spars carry most of the vertical load.

Twist of the combined section compared with the nose cell alone: had the D-cell carried all 40 kN·m, q would be 566 N/mm and the nose skin stress 472 N/mm², far beyond the allowable. The second cell is what makes the torque box work.
A matrix form, [K]{q} = {r}, with one equal-twist row and one torque row, is how a program would solve the same system for any number of cells.

bank.q: A wing box 600 mm × 200 mm has 400 mm² spar caps and 150 mm² stringers at quarter-widths of both skins; skins 1.5 mm, webs 2.5 mm. Idealise it, then find the boom stresses for M<sub>x</sub> = 50 kN·m and the panel shear flows for S<sub>y</sub> = 30 kN on the axis of symmetry.
answer: Data: a wing box 600 mm wide and 200 mm deep (mid-line). Spar caps 400 mm² at the four corners; stringers of 150 mm² at x = 150, 300 and 450 mm on both skins; skins 1.5 mm, spar webs 2.5 mm. M<sub>x</sub> = 50 kN·m and S<sub>y</sub> = 30 kN through the vertical axis of symmetry.
Idealise: every skin panel is 150 mm wide with σ₂/σ₁ = 1; each web is 200 mm deep with σ₂/σ₁ = −1.

answer.text: Boom areas:
Second moment, checked against the real section:
answer.pre:
idealised: (4 × 595.8 + 6 × 375) × 100² = 4.6333 × 10⁷ mm⁴
real: skins 1.8 × 10⁷ + webs 3.333 × 10⁶ + caps 1.6 × 10⁷ + stringers 9 × 10⁶ = 4.6333 × 10⁷ mm⁴

answer: Boom stresses: σ = M y/I = 50 × 10⁶ × 100/4.6333 × 10⁷ = ±107.9 N/mm², the same in every boom on one skin.
Shear: k = S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> = 6.4748 × 10⁻⁴ N/mm³; each stringer jump is k × 375 × 100 = 24.28 N/mm and each corner jump k × 595.8 × 100 = 38.58 N/mm.

Symmetry: the load is on the axis of symmetry and the middle stringer sits on it, so the panels either side of it carry equal and opposite flows of half its jump, 12.14 N/mm. No q<sub>s,0</sub> is needed.

answer.text: Working outwards on the top skin, then down the webs:

answer: The bottom skin mirrors the top. Check: 2 webs × 75.00 × 200 = 30,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>; the web flow equals S/(2h) = 30,000/400 = 75 N/mm, as it must for a box symmetric about both axes.
Stresses: web τ = 75.00/2.5 = 30.0 N/mm²; skin panels next to the spars τ = 36.42/1.5 = 24.3 N/mm².
Sketch: booms as circles, panel flows as arrows: outward from the middle along the top, down both webs, inward along the bottom (for an upward lift on the box the senses reverse).

bank.q: A two-boom cantilever spar 3 m long tapers linearly from 300 mm deep at the root to 150 mm at the tip and carries 8 kN/m along its span. Find the boom force and the web shear flow at the root and at mid-span, allowing for the taper.
outline: Root: P, boom share, web flow
answer: Data: cantilever spar 3 m long with two booms, depth 300 mm at the root and 150 mm at the tip, tapering linearly; a uniform load of 8 kN/m along the span. Find the boom force and the web shear flow at the root and at mid-span.
Taper: the depth falls 150 mm over 3000 mm, h′ = 0.05; each boom slopes at 0.025.

answer.text: Loads at a distance x from the tip:
answer.pre: S = w x,   M = w x²/2,   w = 8 N/mm

answer.text: Root (x = 3000 mm, h = 300 mm):

answer: Without taper the root flow would be S/h = 80.0 N/mm: the taper relieves the web by 25 per cent.

answer.text: Mid-span (x = 1500 mm, h = 225 mm):
Check at the root by boom equilibrium, z outboard, dM/dz = −S:

answer: Why: the boom force acts along the inclined boom, so each boom has a component across the beam; for a beam deepest where the moment is largest both components act with the web against the load.

With the uniform load the boom share falls faster than the shear towards the tip, so here the web flow is largest at the root; with a tip load, as in the chapter example, it is largest at the tip. Each station must be checked.

General form for many booms: S<sub>y,w</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> − Σ P<sub>z,r</sub> δy<sub>r</sub>/δz, with P<sub>z,r</sub> = σ<sub>r</sub> B<sub>r</sub> from the bending stress at the station; then the panel flows follow from the idealised-section sum with S<sub>y,w</sub> in place of S<sub>y</sub>.
Boom stresses for 600 mm² booms: 200 N/mm² at the root and 66.7 N/mm² at mid-span, which shows that boom size is set at the root while the web may be critical elsewhere.

Sign rule to remember: draw both boom forces as arrows along the booms (tension away from the section, compression towards it). If their components across the beam point the same way as the web shear resisting the load, subtract them from S; if they point the other way, add them.
Assumptions: small taper angle (boom force along z ≈ boom force), booms carry all the direct stress, web carries only shear.

bank.q: A wing section has one closed cell and two open trailing panels. Explain how many cuts and constants are needed and write the equations that fix them. Then find the flows, the rate of twist and the shear centre for the section given, with the load at 150 mm behind the front spar.
answer: Set-up: one closed cell with booms 1 (0, 50), 2 (200, 50), 3 (200, −50), 4 (0, −50) mm of 600, 800, 800, 600 mm²; spar webs 2 mm, skins 1.5 mm; two open trailing panels from booms 2 and 3 to free booms 5 (300, 25) and 6 (300, −25) of 200 mm². S<sub>y</sub> = 10 kN acting at x = 150 mm. G = 27 GPa.

Cuts and constants: the trailing panels are open and start from zero at booms 5 and 6, so they need no cut and get no constant. The cell needs one cut (in the top skin 2–1) and one constant q<sub>s,0</sub>. In general: one cut and one constant per closed cell, none for open parts.

answer.text: Equations: with the load position known, moments fix q<sub>s,0</sub> and the twist equation then gives the rate of twist:
answer.pre:
S<sub>y</sub> x<sub>S</sub> = (moments of q<sub>b</sub> about O) + 2A q<sub>s,0</sub>
dθ/dz = (1/2AG) ∮ (q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>s,0</sub>) ds/t   (cell walls only)

answer: I<sub>xx</sub> = 7,250,000 mm⁴ (all six booms). Basic flows: trailing panels 6.90 N/mm; front spar −41.38 N/mm (downwards along s, so upwards physically); rear spar 62.07 N/mm upwards; skins zero.
Moments of q<sub>b</sub> about the front-spar mid-point: 1,103,448 N·mm.
Moment equation with the load at 150 mm: 10,000 × 150 = 1,103,448 + 40,000 q<sub>s,0</sub>, so q<sub>s,0</sub> = 9.91 N/mm.
Final flows: front spar 31.47 N/mm upwards, rear spar 71.98 N/mm upwards, skins 9.91 N/mm; trailing panels unchanged at 6.90 N/mm. Check: 100 × (31.47 + 71.98) − 2 × 172.4 = 10,000 N.
Twist: ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds/t = 1,034.5, ∮ds/t = 366.67; dθ/dz = (1,034.5 + 9.91 × 366.67)/(2 × 20,000 × 27,000) = 4.324 × 10⁻⁶ rad/mm, anticlockwise, because the load is now behind the shear centre.

Shear centre: setting dθ/dz = 0 gives q<sub>s,0</sub> = −1,034.5/366.67 = −2.821 N/mm and x<sub>S</sub> = (1,103,448 + 40,000 × (−2.821))/10,000 = 99.1 mm. The load at 150 mm is 50.9 mm behind it, consistent with the sign of the twist.
Two cells sharing a wall would add a second constant and an equal-twist equation; the shared wall carries q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>s,0,1</sub> − q<sub>s,0,2</sub>.
Common errors: putting a constant into an open panel; leaving the open booms out of I<sub>xx</sub>; using the twist equation of an open part.

bank.q: Evaluate open sections, single closed cells and multi-cell boxes for use as a wing torque box, using torsional stiffness, stress, fail-safety and weight. Support the argument with numbers.
answer: Criterion: a torque box must carry the wing torque with low twist (aileron effectiveness, divergence and flutter margins) and acceptable shear stress, at low weight.

answer.text: Open section. J = Σbt³/3 depends on the cube of the thickness. For a 2 mm strip 120 mm long formed into a 60 mm angle under 10 N·m:
answer.pre: J = 320 mm⁴,  τ<sub>max</sub> = 62.5 N/mm²,  twist 66.3° per metre

answer.text: Single closed cell. The same strip closed into a 30 mm square tube:
answer.pre:
J = 4A²/∮ds/t = 54,000 mm⁴,  τ = 2.78 N/mm²,  twist 0.393° per metre
stiffness ratio 169, stress ratio 22.5

answer: The closed cell wins because its shear flow acts round the whole enclosed area, with a lever arm of the section size, while the open section's stresses act across the thickness only.

Multi-cell. Splitting a box with a middle spar barely changes the total enclosed area, so the stiffness changes little; the gain is in redundancy and in shorter, more stable skin panels. In the two-cell example of the multi-cell chapter, 20 kN·m twists the box 1.749° per metre and the shared wall carries only 17.4 N/mm.

Fail-safety. If one cell of a multi-cell box is cracked, the remaining cell still carries torque by Bredt–Batho flow; a single cell cracked along its length becomes an open section and loses almost all its stiffness.

Weight. For a given torque and allowable stress the closed cell needs t = T/(2Aτ), so its weight is set by the enclosed area, which is fixed by the aerofoil. The open section would need walls many times thicker to reach the same twist.

Practical points: cut-outs for undercarriage or access turn a closed bay into an open one and need doublers or heavy ribs; open stringers are kept for bending stiffness and to stabilise the skin, not for torque.
Shear centre: a closed box has its shear centre inside the box, near the line of the main loads; an open channel has it outside the web, so loads naturally miss it.

Conclusion: the wing torque box should be closed, usually with two or three cells, with open stringers and ribs supporting the skin; open sections are evaluated for torsion only where they cannot be avoided (control-surface spars, stringer run-outs) and are kept short or closed locally.

bank.q: Explain Wagner's complete tension field theory for a thin-webbed beam. For a cantilever with flanges 300 mm apart (350 mm² each), a 0.8 mm web, 150 mm² stiffeners at 250 mm and a 15 kN tip load, find α, σ<sub>t</sub>, the flange loads 1 m from the tip, the stiffener load and the flange secondary moment.
answer: Concept: a thin web loaded in shear has principal tension and compression on its two 45° diagonals. It buckles under the compression at τ<sub>cr</sub> and carries further load as tension along the wrinkles, the diagonal tension field. Wagner's complete tension field assumes the buckling stress is negligible.
Data: cantilever, flanges 300 mm apart (A<sub>F</sub> = 350 mm² each), web 0.8 mm, stiffeners of 150 mm² every 250 mm, tip load W = 15 kN, section 1 m from the tip; E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33.

Buckling check: k<sub>s</sub> = 5.35 + 4(250/300)² = 8.13; τ<sub>cr</sub> = 8.13 × π² × 70,000 × (0.8/250)²/(12 × 0.891) = 5.38 N/mm², against a nominal τ = W/(t d) = 62.5 N/mm². The web buckles early, and the complete field is a fair model.

answer.text: Angle of the field:
Diagonal tension, from vertical equilibrium of a vertical cut (σ<sub>t</sub> t d sin α cos α = W):
Flange loads: bending W z/d plus half the horizontal field component W/tan α as compression in each:
answer.pre:
W z/d = 15,000 × 1000/300 = 50,000 N
W/(2 tan α) = 8,611 N
F<sub>T</sub> = 41,389 N (tension),  F<sub>B</sub> = −58,611 N (compression)

answer.text: Stiffener load, from the field pulling the flanges together:
answer.pre:
P = σ<sub>t</sub> t b sin²α = W b tan α/d = 15,000 × 250 × 0.8710/300 = 10,887 N
stress 72.6 N/mm² in compression

answer.text: Flange secondary bending between stiffeners, under the distributed pull W tan α/d:
answer.pre: M = W b² tan α/(12 d) = 226,820 N·mm at each stiffener,  113,410 N·mm midway

answer: Shear flow: the web still delivers q = W/d = 50 N/mm to the flanges on average; what changes is the route, through tension along the wrinkles instead of pure shear.

Design consequences: the compression flange is loaded more than bending says; the stiffeners are struts and must be checked for column buckling; the flanges must carry the secondary bending; rivets along the flanges carry the field.
If τ<sub>cr</sub> is not small, part of the shear stays as flat-web shear, and incomplete tension field methods share the load; Wagner's field is then conservative for flanges and stiffeners.
